title: Integrity constraints
summary: Domain, key, referential, and check constraints say which writes are legal. ON DELETE CASCADE removes the referencing child rows when the parent goes; ON DELETE RESTRICT refuses the parent delete.
intuition:
An integrity constraint is a rule every instance has to satisfy, checked when a row is inserted, updated, or deleted. A domain constraint keeps each value inside the attribute's domain: an integer column rejects a string, and a domain of positive integers rejects a negative age. A check constraint is a predicate on the row being written, such as $0\le \mathrm{hours}\le 24$. It does not go and look in another table.

Entity integrity is the primary-key rule. The primary key is unique, and none of its attributes is null. Inserting a second row with an existing key, or inserting a null into the key, violates it. A referential constraint is the foreign-key rule. A non-null foreign key must equal the candidate key of some row in the referenced table. Inserting an employee whose department id matches no department violates it. Inserting a new department does not, because nothing is required to point at a parent before the parent exists.

Deletes are the case that needs a direction. If a child row points at a parent, deleting the parent would leave a foreign key that matches nothing. ON DELETE RESTRICT refuses that parent delete: the statement fails, and both the parent and the children stay. ON DELETE CASCADE does the opposite of "delete the parent because a child disappeared." When the parent row is deleted, the database deletes the child rows that reference it. The children go because the parent went. Deleting a child, who is referenced by nobody, does not delete the parent. ON DELETE SET NULL is a third action, usable only when the foreign key may be null: the children stay and the foreign key is set to null.

definitions.body: Every value of an attribute belongs to the declared domain. A type failure, or a value outside an enumerated domain, violates it on insert or update. It is checked on the value itself.
The primary key is unique and not null. A duplicate key or a null key on insert or update violates it. This is the key constraint of the primary key.

Every non-null foreign-key value equals the referenced candidate key of an existing row. Inserting a dangling key violates it. Deleting a referenced parent violates it unless a delete action removes or rewrites the children.

CASCADE: deleting a parent deletes the child rows that reference it. RESTRICT: if any child references the parent, the parent delete is rejected and no row is removed. Neither action deletes a parent because a child was deleted.

formulas.name: Foreign key after a parent delete
formulas.note: The trigger is the deletion of the referenced parent. Child rows are the referencing rows.

formulas.name: Entity integrity
formulas.note: Both halves are required. A unique column that allows null is not a primary key.

properties: A domain violation is a bad value. A check violation is a row that fails a predicate. Neither one consults another table.
Entity integrity rejects a duplicate primary key and a null primary key. Referential integrity rejects a non-null foreign key that matches no parent.
ON DELETE CASCADE deletes referencing child rows when the parent row is deleted. It does not delete the parent when a child row is deleted.
ON DELETE RESTRICT rejects the parent delete while any child still references that parent. The children are not deleted to make the statement succeed.

Deleting a child that nothing else references does not violate referential integrity. Deleting a parent that is still referenced does, unless CASCADE, SET NULL, or another declared action handles the children.

examples.title: Three inserts, three different constraints
examples.prompt: Dept ids are $1$ and $2$. Emp(id, dept_id) currently holds $(10,1)$, $(11,1)$, and $(12,2)$. The primary key is id. dept_id references Dept and may not be null. A separate check says $0\le \mathrm{hours}\le 24$ on a timesheet row. Classify the writes.
steps: Inserting Emp $(13, 9)$ uses a fresh primary key and a dept_id that is not in Dept. The primary key is fine. Referential integrity fails.

Inserting Emp $(10, 2)$ reuses the primary key $10$. Entity integrity fails, even though department $2$ exists. Inserting Emp $(\mathrm{NULL}, 1)$ also fails entity integrity, because a primary key may not be null.
Inserting a timesheet row with hours $30$ for employee $10$ passes the key and the foreign key, and fails the check $0\le \mathrm{hours}\le 24$. The check does not look at Dept.
examples.answer: dept_id $9$ violates referential integrity. A repeated or null id violates entity integrity. hours $30$ violates the check constraint.

examples.title: Delete department 1, two actions
examples.prompt: The same Emp rows reference departments. Two employees point at department $1$, and one points at department $2$. Delete department $1$ under ON DELETE CASCADE, and again under ON DELETE RESTRICT.
steps: Under CASCADE the parent delete is what the statement asked for. The database then deletes the child rows whose dept_id is $1$, namely employees $10$ and $11$. Employee $12$ points at department $2$ and stays. One employee row remains.
The direction is parent to children. The delete of department $1$ is not caused by deleting an employee. After the cascade, department $1$ is gone and its former children are gone with it.

Under RESTRICT a child still references department $1$, so the delete is rejected. Departments $1$ and $2$ stay, and all three employee rows stay. Restrict does not delete the two children in order to save the statement.
examples.answer: CASCADE leaves $1$ employee row. RESTRICT leaves $3$ employee rows and does not delete the department.

traps: Reversing CASCADE. The parent delete removes the referencing children. Deleting a child does not cascade upward and delete the parent.
Thinking RESTRICT deletes the children and then deletes the parent. RESTRICT refuses the parent delete and leaves every row in place.
Calling a check failure a foreign-key failure. hours $30$ can violate a check while both the primary key and the foreign key are legal.
Allowing a null primary key because the foreign key permits null. Entity integrity forbids null in the primary key even when other columns may be null.

questions.stem: Emp(id, dept_id) has primary key id, and dept_id references Dept. Dept contains ids $1$ and $2$. Inserting Emp $(13, 9)$ violates
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, referential integrity.

The primary key $13$ is new and not null, so entity integrity holds. There is no department $9$, so the foreign key matches nothing. The row has no salary and no name to blame on a check or a domain of those other columns.
options: entity integrity, because $13$ is a new key
a check on a salary column this row does not contain
a domain constraint on a name this row does not contain

questions.stem: Department $1$ is referenced by two employee rows. Deleting that department under ON DELETE RESTRICT
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**.

RESTRICT rejects the parent delete while a child row still references it. No employee is removed, and the department stays. Option B is ON DELETE CASCADE, whose direction is the opposite: the children are deleted because the parent was deleted. RESTRICT does not rewrite foreign keys and does not touch employees of other departments.
options: is rejected, and the employee rows stay
deletes those two employees and then the department
deletes the department and sets the two foreign keys to $0$
deletes every employee in the database

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

Entity integrity is uniqueness plus the ban on null in the primary key. A domain constraint rejects a value outside the attribute's domain. ON DELETE CASCADE, fired by the deletion of a parent, deletes the child rows that reference it. Option D reverses that direction. A child delete does not cascade up to the parent.
options: Entity integrity says the primary key is unique and not null.
A domain constraint rejects a value outside the attribute's domain.
ON DELETE CASCADE deletes referencing child rows when the parent row is deleted.
ON DELETE CASCADE deletes the parent because a child row was deleted.

questions.stem: Dept contains $1$ and $2$. Emp contains $(10,1)$, $(11,1)$, and $(12,2)$, with primary key id and foreign key dept_id. Which of the following are true?
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

Inserting $(10, 2)$ repeats the primary key $10$, which violates entity integrity even though department $2$ exists. Inserting a null primary key violates entity integrity. Under CASCADE, deleting department $1$ deletes employees $10$ and $11$ and leaves employee $12$, so one employee row remains. Option D is the RESTRICT outcome only if the delete succeeded; RESTRICT rejects it and leaves all three employees.
options: Under ON DELETE CASCADE, deleting department $1$ leaves exactly one employee row.
Under ON DELETE RESTRICT, deleting department $1$ leaves exactly one employee row.

questions.stem: A table has $40$ employee rows, and $7$ of them reference department $D$. Department $D$ is deleted under ON DELETE CASCADE. How many employee rows remain?
questions.solution:
The answer is **33**.

CASCADE deletes the child rows that reference the deleted parent, and no others. Removing those $7$ rows from $40$ leaves $40-7=33$ employee rows. The other departments' employees are not children of $D$.
